低音巴松管的前身可追溯至1590年奧地利與德國，因加倍低音線需求出現較低八度杜爾: The forerunner of the contrabassoon can be traced to Austria and Germany in 1590, when the need to double the bass line produced a dulcian an octave lower; by 1626 there is a record of a contrafagott in use in Frankfurt. At the end of the seventeenth century France and England developed their own Baroque forerunners, and by the middle of the eighteenth century, especially in England, the instrument took shape; the earliest surviving instruments, from 1714, have only four parts and three keys, and it entered church music. Bach's St John Passion and Handel's L'Allegro and Music for the Royal Fireworks all show early use. Until the end of the nineteenth century the tone and intonation were weak and the serpent and bass sarrusophone were often substituted; Heckel's improvements established it as standard, and since 2000 a new key system has appeared.

In the bass the vibration of the large reed and the bell produce a powerful low register; at louder volumes it often has a buzz or a tremor, an effect that the reed design can reduce or keep. The very top of its range thins out and is less penetrating than the oboe or the bassoon, and is easily covered by the other parts. The range is about three octaves, from B-flat0 (on some instruments down to A0) upwards, and the highest notes are rarely used.

The contrabassoon (H-S 422.112-71) is a European double-reed aerophone of the bassoon family, sounding an octave below the bassoon. Its tube is longer and folds back twice, it is supported on a peg, the reed is larger, the finger holes are further apart, and the key system is simplified but keeps the water key and the tuning slide. It is played much like the bassoon, and the fingering in the low register is almost the same, while the high register differs. It is used mainly in symphony orchestras and wind bands, usually played as a double by a bassoonist, and in large works it doubles the bass with the tuba and the bass trombone.
多見於交響樂團與管樂團，常作為木管組最低聲部，在大型交響作品中與低音長號或低音號: It is mostly found in symphony orchestras and wind bands, often as the lowest voice of the woodwind group, doubling the bass trombone or tuba at the octave in large orchestral works. Beethoven's Fifth Symphony has an independent part for it, and the fourth movement of the Ninth also supplies the bass; Handel's Royal Fireworks, Haydn's The Creation and Mozart's Coronation Mass use it too. Ravel's Mother Goose suite and Holst's The Planets have solos for it; Dukas's The Sorcerer's Apprentice and Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring need two. Among modern works there are concertos by Schuller, Elbe and Aho.
演奏低音巴松管時，因管體長且重，通常以底部金屬腳棒支撐，必要時再加頸帶；吹嘴與部: Because the tube is long and heavy, the contrabassoon is usually supported on a metal peg at the bottom, with a neck strap added if needed; the bocal, and on some models the bell, can be taken off, while most of the rest is pre-fitted. Sound depends on the vibration of the large double reed, and how the reed is scraped affects intonation, timbre and response. A beginner can first check the assembly and adjust the tuning slide, and drain the water with the water key before playing. The fingering in the low register is close to the bassoon's, a different fingering has to be learned from the second register up, and the high register is quite different; the main key spacing is wider and the hands have to open out.
